entries.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
entries.summary: From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.
entries.content:
HistoryGlobal issues

From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible

July 31, 2026

From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

It was a clip destined to go viral.

On July 22, 2026, in rainy Mumbai, a casually dressed young woman stepped in front of a slow-moving police van carrying detained students.

She placed her palm on the hood, forcing the vehicle to stop. Mobile phones captured the moment from every angle. She too, raised her own phone and recorded the encounter.

Within hours, the clip spread across India and beyond.

It became one of the defining visuals of the Cockroach Janta Party protests, in which students demanded transparency and accountability, following leaks in India's medical entrance exams.

But the power of the moment lay not only in what she did, but in how quickly it was seen. A single gesture, a young woman confronting authority, became a symbol shared across millions of screens.

While the clip belongs to a generation raised on social media, the impulse behind it is much older.

From court petitions and revolutionary posters to photographs, umbrellas and memes, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols available to them, turning them into vehicles for dissent.

Communicating dissent at court

Long before television or social media carried dissent across borders, students still found ways to make their grievances heard.

In Eastern Han China for instance, scholars at the Imperial Academy (Taixue) aligned with reform-minded officials in opposing powerful eunuchs at court, whom many viewed as corrupt and politically overbearing.

They voiced their objections through public criticism, political networks and petitions.

In an era when political communication moved through official channels, petitions were among the established ways of bringing grievances before the throne. Written in formal language and delivered through the bureaucracy, they carried student concerns directly into the state's communication system.

Multiplying dissent through posters

Centuries later, communication and protest mechanisms evolved.

In Paris in 1968, students challenged university authorities and a conservative postwar social order. As demonstrations spread across the French capital and drew in workers, one of the movement's most enduring contributions emerged from a basement workshop at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts.

The Atelier Populaire ("People's Workshop") printed thousands of posters during the protests, many of them overnight. Their bold graphics, silhouettes and slogans became the visual language of the movement. Produced collectively, many carried no individual author's name, helping transform protest into a shared public voice.

The posters and their messages could appear in dozens of places overnight, giving the protest a wide local visual presence.

When a photograph became global witness

Protests also became more impactful when images could be transmitted across borders.

In Soweto in June 1976, Black South African students marched against the apartheid system's education policies, rejecting Afrikaans as a compulsory medium of instruction in Black schools. Many saw it as the language of an oppressive state and a barrier to equal education.

As thousands of students took to the streets, police opened fire. Amid the chaos, South African photographer Sam Nzima captured the image that would travel the world: 13-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried away from the scene after he was fatally shot.

The photograph became one of the defining images of apartheid. For many outside South Africa, it served as the lens through which the students' protest was seen and understood, helping build international awareness of and opposition to apartheid.

When images become iconic

In the spring of 1989, students gathered in Beijing's Tiananmen Square demanding democratic reforms, freedom of expression and an end to corruption. As the protests grew, so did the need for symbols that could communicate their message beyond the square.

In the final weeks of the occupation of Tiananmen Square, students built the Goddess of Democracy. Facing Mao Zedong's portrait, the 10-meter statue became a powerful symbol of the movement.

But while the students created one icon, history would produce another. After the brutal military crackdown on the protesters, a photograph of a lone man, later known as "Tank Man," standing facing a column of tanks traveled around the world.

Global media did not create these symbols, but amplified them. Cameras, newspapers and broadcasters transformed these local acts of defiance into enduring images of resistance.

From organizers to participants

Over time, protest communication no longer flowed only from organizers outward. Crowds and bystanders increasingly helped shape it.

In Chile in 2011, students demanding education reform used flash mobs, performances and public spectacle to draw attention to their cause. Protest was no longer just something people watched. It became something they could join.

In Hong Kong in 2014, students protesting Beijing's plans for electoral reform transformed everyday objects into political symbols. And what began as a practical response to pepper spray and tear gas soon became the defining image of the Umbrella Movement.

Modeled on Prague's original John Lennon Wall that was created after his murder in 1988 and went on to provide a space for people to express irritation with the communist regime, Lennon Walls in Hong Kong also became hubs of public expression, attracting thousands of people who left messages of support and protest on sticky notes attached to walls around the city.

From slur to symbol

And then there are the political platforms that shape which symbols become widely seen, as is the case in India recently.

Students protesting exam irregularities took an insult aimed at them and made it their own: "Cockroach" quickly became one of the movement's most recognizable symbols online.

Memes and reels often spread faster than official statements, with students using them to respond to criticism, mock their opponents and rally support.

Like posters in Paris or umbrellas in Hong Kong, this particular instance shows how memes can transform a disparaging label into a powerful protest symbol.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
entries.summary: The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots — a market dominated by Chinese tech firms. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots — a market dominated by Chinese tech firms. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.

In the latest sign of China's threat to the United States' tech dominance, the Trump administration on Tuesday banned new foreign-made humanoid and four-legged robotsfrom entering the country.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cited "unacceptable risks" to national security for the decision.

The FCC noted how the robots "collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots."

The move is widely seen as aimed squarely at China, which accounted for 85% of humanoid robot deployments last year, according to British bank Barclays.

How serious is the security threat from Chinese robots?

US officials warn that Chinese humanoid and quadruped (four-legged) robots can collect detailed location and personal data, be controlled remotely and pose risks for critical US infrastructure.

Specific concerns center on the robots' potential dual-use — civilian and military purposes.

Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese robot maker, appears on the Pentagon's list of firms with links to the Chinese military. Its robots have been used in army exercises.

Researchers have also shown that Unitree robots have security flaws that let attackers take control with a voice command and then use one robot to control others.

Washington is also concerned that a large cohort of low-cost Chinese robots could feed real-world data back to Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which are fast catching up with their US rivals.

The threat, however, is largely theoretical as most commercial humanoid robots are in early stages of development.

China has rejected the accusations, insisting Washington is using national security as a pretext for protectionism to suppress Chinese technology.

Beijing is expected to impose countermeasures, which could include curbs on the raw materials US robotics firms urgently need to scale up production.

The Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to help the domestic US robotics industry, which in turn supports the country's nearly trillion-dollar AI buildout.

According to industry watchers, US President Donald Trump wants to ensure the likes of Figure AI, Tesla Optimus and Agility Robotics are protected from high-volume Chinese producers, whose robots often cost half the price or less of their US rivals.

Washington has put similar curbs on Chinese drones and solar panels and now levies a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.

Will the ban help US robot makers catch up?

The ban is widely seen as an attempt by Washington to buy time, having been caught off guard by how quickly China scaled robotics production.

According to Omdia, a tech research house, China has six firms in the Top 10 robotics rankings and they shipped nearly 11,600 humanoids last year, versus a few hundred by US firms.

In March, Bank of America forecast around 90,000 shipments by the end of this year.

The US is widely seen as stronger at making a robot's brain smart through advanced AI, while China leads at mass-producing cheaper robots with bodies that move better thanks to high-performance actuators or robotic muscles.

Rush Doshi, director of the Initiative on China Strategy at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the ban as "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the US robotics ecosystem."

Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, a maker of robot arms, thinks the Trump administration is sending an "unambiguous" message to Beijing.

"Robotics is a technology America must lead and own — and foreign-subsidized robots will not be allowed to unfairly dominate US robotics..." Beard wrote on X.

Critics, however, think the ban could slow US AI innovation as researchers currently benefit from being able to run tests on budget-friendly Chinese robots.

"Restrictions can reduce security exposure, but they do not by themselves create a competitive domestic ecosystem," Georg Stieler, an advisor to the robotics industry, wrote on X.

US business channel CNBC cited Marc Einstein, a research director at Counterpoint Research, as saying the ban was "bad news for Chinese humanoid producers planning their IPOs in the coming months."

Einstein warned that Beijing could now "further restrict rare earth sales to American companies and … Chinese market access for American companies like Tesla and Nvidia."

How big could humanoid robots become?

Barclays estimates the market, currently worth just $2 to 3 billion (€1.7 to 2.6 billion), could reach $200 billion by 2035 in the most optimistic scenario, if the robot's brains, brawn and batteries can be improved.

Elon Musk is even more bullish, saying Tesla's Optimus could become "the biggest product ever" with long-term sales potentially reaching $10 trillion.

At scale, he believes the robots, which currently sell for about $100,000, could eventually cost $20,000 to $30,000 each — cheap enough for factories, warehouses and later homes.

Combining Barclays' forecast with Musk's target price points to roughly 7 to 10 million humanoid robots being sold each year by 2035.

In the near term, humanoids are expected to take on repetitive and physically demanding jobs in warehouses and factories. Later, they could expand into health, elderly care and household chores.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Germany news: Unemployment tops 3 million as industry slumps
entries.summary: Over three million people are currently unemployed in Germany, with 1.1 million drawing unemployment checks, authorities say. Also, sales of air conditioners have doubled as heat continues to crush cities. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Unemployment tops 3 million as industry slumps

Published July 31, 2026last updated July 31, 2026

Over three million people are currently unemployed in Germany, with 1.1 million drawing unemployment checks, authorities say. Also, sales of air conditioners have doubled as heat continues to crush cities. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's employment agency recorded a jump of 71,000 in monthly unemployment numbers, pushing the total to over 3 million

  • EU's biggest economy reports 6.4% overall unemployment rate

  • Sales of portable air conditioners in Germany doubled in the first six months of 2026, according to market researcher NIQ

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on Friday, July 31, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Germans go crazy for portable A/C units, doubling year-on-year sales

Germans go crazy for portable A/C units, doubling year-on-year sales

As summers continue to get hotter, Germans' appetite for air conditioners has grown exponentially. 

According to the US market researcher NielsenIQ, or NIQ, German consumers purchased some 387,100 portable air-conditioning units in the first half of 2026 — an increase 219,000 units or 130% over Q1/2 2025.

May saw a 238% year-on-year sales increase and June — when a heatwave swept the country — a 121% jump in which 290,000 units were sold, 159,000 units more than the same month in 2025.

NIQ, which shared its market analytics data with German news agency DPA, said the units sold cost roughly €350 ($400) and were of two types: Transportable inside units that pump moisture out of doors via a small tube, as well as so-called split units consisting of interior and exterior elements.

The latter, more powerful type has gained significantly in popularity say NIQ analysts.

NIQ experts cited price, availability and easy operation as sales points for portable units, though they noted that these lack the efficiency and comfort of larger, fixed installation A/C systems, which were not included in the data.

Skip next section Unemployment tops three million

Unemployment tops three million

Germany's Federal Employment Agency (BA) released its July unemployment numbers on Friday, showing an increase in joblessness. July's numbers jumped 71,000 over June, and 28,000 compared to July 2025.

"Unemployment and underemployment tend to jump significantly in July due to seasonal factors," said AB board member Daniel Terzenbach in Nuremberg. "Overall, this is a continuation of the weak labor market trends seen in recent months."

The seasonal dip has to do with the fact that apprenticeships tend to end in summer, leaving young people temporarily unemployed. Businesses also tend to postpone hiring until after the summer break.

Total unemployment now stands at 6.4% (up 0.2% from June), with some 3,007 million in Germany without work — the first time unemployment has pushed past three million since April.

Demand for workers was also lower in July according to the BA, which registered 653,000 advertised job openings, though that is 25,000 more than at the same time in 2025. 

The number of people drawing unemployment checks also increased by 107,000 to 1.108 million; and statistics put the number of able-bodied welfare recipients at 3.775 million, down 121,000 compared to July 2025.

Not all of those receiving welfare were unemployed, with some working to reach minimum subsistence levels.

Employment agencies however also registered an increase in the number of people looking to enter apprenticeships — 418,000, up 4,000 from July 2025.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW news in Bonn where temperatures are not as high as feared but it's plenty muggy.

Today we'll kick off with monthly unemployment numbers, which are up. This is not too surprising in terms of seasonal trends — unemployment always jumps in July. Still, the number are also higher than last year. The Federal Employment Agency says this reflects the generally weak state of the German labor market.

Those Germans with money to spare, however, are buying portable air conditioners at double last year's rates. The units are flying off the shelves wie warme Semmeln (like warm rolls… as opposed to hotcakes) as Europe bakes.

A majority of Germans (83%) also feel that municipalities are doing too little to protect citizens from the dangers of extreme heat, with many calling for more public drinking fountains, cool spaces and more urban greenery — tell that to your neighbor with the new paved garden in front of their double carport! 

Interestingly, political affiliation appeared to play little or no role in people's opinions about protection against the heat — despite the ideological battles being waged for years over the concept of climate change. When it's hot, it's hot, it seems, no matter your political persuasion.

Follow DW here for the latest Germany news throughout the day.

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
entries.summary: A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the border zone that divided East and West Germany was left largely untouched. Today, the nearly 1,400-kilometer (870 miles) stretch, once known as the death strip, is a "green belt." It's home to around 7,500 species of insects and spiders, hundreds of them endangered, as well as otters, wildcats and birds on the brink of extinction.

Because the military zone was sealed off for decades, species that have vanished elsewhere in Germany were able to take hold here. Now 88% of the area is under protection, and cycle paths and information panels allow visitors to explore what was once completely off-limits.

Read the full story here: East-West border death zone now Germany's biodiversity oasis 

An urban tree database

Not all heroes wear capes, but some do form a canopy. Urban trees quietly cool neighborhoods, reduce flooding, and improve our wellbeing. But in many cities, trees are under pressure from heat, drought, traffic and too much concrete.

Now, a citizen-science project in Germany is helping people map and monitor the trees around them. Think Pokemon Go, but for urban nature and with real-world benefits for the climate.

Seagrass goes from beach nuisance to building material

On Poel, a German island in the Baltic Sea, washed-up seagrass is being turned into sustainable insulation for homes, while helping clean local beaches in the process.

As demand for eco-friendly construction materials grows, the project is attracting interest from across Europe and could give new value to a resource that was previously viewed as waste.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Small insects, big damage: The global ant trade is booming
entries.summary: Legal or not, the trade in African ants bound for Europe is booming. What do hobbyists find appealing about these insects, and what risks does the trade pose to ecosystems, including power outages?
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

Legal or not, the trade in African ants bound for Europe is booming. What do hobbyists find appealing about these insects, and what risks does the trade pose to ecosystems, including power outages?

They are unusual pieces of evidence that regularly appear in Kenyan courtrooms: thousands of ants packed into tiny containers.

Since 2025, such finds have been presented in court several times. Staff from the Kenya Wildlife Service discovered them during baggage inspections. In multiple cases, they identified thousands of specimens of the sought-after Messor Cephalotes species also known as the Giant African Harvester Ant. A single queen can fetch more than €200 ($230) on the market.

The export of wild animals is generally prohibited in Kenya. Due to high levels of poaching — particularly involving elephants and rhinoceroses — many African countries have introduced tough laws against wildlife trafficking.

Kenya has also tightened its legislation. Under these rules, a Chinese national who attempted to export ants was sentenced last April to one year in prison for biopiracy. Given the growing scale of smuggling and its ecological consequences, the judge said the sentence should serve as a deterrent.

It was already the second major ant-smuggling case in 12 months. The previous year, the wildlife service stopped four men who referred to themselves as the "Ant Gang." Among them were two 19-year-old Belgians who were trying to smuggle 5,500 queens to Europe. They were fined around €5,000 each.

Whenever such cases arise, authorities often call entomologist Dino Martins to the airport. "I was shocked," he said. "Not only by the sheer number of ants, but also because they were queen ants."

The seized insects were young queens that had been dug up from nests in the ground, according to Martins, who has led several research institutes in Kenya and is regarded as one of Africa's leading ant experts, These queens have wings that allow them to fly away and establish new colonies.

"When you collect queens at this critical moment, you interrupt a key stage in the creation of new colonies," he said, adding that Kenya's ecosystems are also affected because ants transport grass seeds, helping to regenerate the savannah.

A new niche hobby

In Europe, keeping ants as pets has become increasingly popular, particularly among young people. Colonies are housed in glass terrariums where a queen produces offspring and establishes an entirely new population.

One person who keeps ants as a hobby is Michael Meier, who asked not to be identified by his real name. While at university, he wanted a pet that required little attention.

"With ants, it doesn't really matter whether I feed them today or tomorrow," he said.

At one point, Meier kept almost 30 colonies in a room specially set up for them. Today, he has four. He admits that exotic species are considered especially attractive to ant enthusiasts because they do not hibernate.

"That way, you can enjoy the animals all year round," he said.

On the websites of numerous online shops, ants can be ordered through the mail with just a few clicks. "African ants" is a category commonly used to attract customers. Among the species on sale is the very one repeatedly discovered at Kenyan airports.

Anyone who asks dealers how the ants reach Europe receives few answers. Even sellers who advertise "import permits" have declined to answer media inquiries. The trade operates in a legal gray area.

Under the international wildlife trade agreement monitored by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), ants are not considered a threatened species. Their trade is therefore neither prohibited nor regulated globally.

Kenya, meanwhile, bans the export of all wildlife. But unlike ivory, ants can easily be smuggled out of the country in hand luggage or through the mail.

High profits, low risk

The online trade in wildlife has expanded rapidly beyond the ant business, says Russell Gray. Working with an international team, he investigated the issue for the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

"The key finding is that this is no longer a marginal problem hidden away on obscure websites," Gray said. "Today, we see it happening on popular platforms such as Facebook."

Last year, Gray's team examined more than 60 online platforms. They found 266,000 advertisements that included prices. The combined value of wildlife listings amounted to around $66 million. Insects were not even included.

"If we looked at the entire online wildlife trade," Gray concludes, "we would probably be talking about a market worth billions."

Chris Shepherd, a biologist at the US-based Center for Biological Diversity, which advocates globally for biodiversity conservation, is deeply concerned.

The Kenyan cases demonstrate that compared with other forms of crime, such as drug trafficking, profits are high while "the risks are significantly lower," he said. Once rare species begin commanding high prices, organized criminal networks become interested in the trade.

Shepherd therefore calls for stricter regulation. In open letters, he has urged CITES to address the ant trade. He is particularly concerned about the consequences for ecosystems.

Ants have no lobby

Those consequences are already making headlines in Germany.

Entire colonies of North African large gland ants regularly cause power and internet outages in southern Germany by nesting inside electrical distribution boxes.

To address the issue, local government representatives from Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany met at an ant conference in the summer of 2025 to exchange experiences.

Climate change, bringing higher temperatures and less frost, has made conditions in Central Europe increasingly suitable for the species.

Shepherd notes that most ants probably arrive in Europe through plant imports rather than the online pet trade. Even so, he argues that the hobby market poses risks as well. No one can guarantee that colonies will never be released into the wild.

Ant keepers such as Meier are familiar with these debates, which frequently take place in online forums. Meier advises owners who lose interest to either pass colonies on to other enthusiasts or euthanize them properly rather than releasing them.

For Shepherd, that is not enough. As long as the international ant trade remains largely unregulated, he says, it will continue to pose a risk.

Translated from German by Silja Fröhlich

entries.title: India's 'Cockroach' protesters face ongoing legal pressure
entries.summary: After forcing the resignation of India's education minister, student activists say a crackdown continues despite government promises to drop criminal cases against protesters.
entries.content:
India

India's 'Cockroach' protesters face ongoing legal pressure

July 31, 2026

After forcing the resignation of India's education minister, student activists say a crackdown continues despite government promises to drop criminal cases against protesters.

A student-led protest movement in Indiasatirically called the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) scored a major political win when Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down after weeks of protests calling for his removal.

The movement began on social media as an activist campaign sparked by leaks of a question sheet for the NEET exam, a highly competitive entrance test for aspiring medical students, in early May.

Along with the education minister stepping down, the government promised to withdraw police cases against peaceful protesters, compensate families affected by the NEET examination controversy and continue talks on the movement's five-point charter for reforming India's examination system.

Now, student leaders, lawyers and activists say the battle has shifted from the streets to police stations, courtrooms and social media.

Indian lawyer and politician Kapil Sibal told DW that the government's actions after the movement called off further protests have raised fresh questions about whether its public assurances are being honored.

"The way Dharmendra Pradhan was celebrated after his resignation shows the government has learned nothing from the protests or the message the students were trying to convey," Sibal said.

Authorities seek legal wiggle room with protesters

The agreement that ended the protests appeared straightforward. Governments in Delhi, Bihar, Assam, Maharashtra and West Bengal announced that protest-related police cases would be withdrawn and detained students released.

But some of those orders included an important caveat. The protection does not extend to protesters whom police describe as having "criminal antecedents," a condition that student leaders say was never discussed during negotiations.

Senior advocate Rebecca Mammen John told DW that government assurances alone do not automatically end criminal proceedings.

"There is a prescribed legal process for withdrawing criminal cases. An oral assurance from the government counts for nothing unless that process is followed," John said.

"Ultimately, it is the courts that decide whether prosecutions are withdrawn or whether police cases are closed."

For the CJP, that legal distinction has become a new battleground. Its leaders argue the "criminal antecedents" clause risks leaving room for selective prosecution even after the movement agreed to suspend its protests.

Government officials, meanwhile, insist peaceful protesters have nothing to fear and that investigations will continue only against those accused of violence or other criminal offenses.

India's Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, said that both police and protesters would be held accountable for violations of the law.

"Whoever has committed excesses and taken [the law into their own hands], and whoever has committed atrocities, they must be brought under the law," the court said in a hearing on Tuesday regarding the police response to the protests . 

A legal battle continues

Sibal told DW that the government's position before the courts appears inconsistent with the commitments it made while negotiating with the students.

"On the one hand, the government promised that no cases would be foisted on students. On the other, investigations against those said to have criminal records continue," he said.

"Who allowed criminal elements to enter the protests? Who allowed trucks carrying stones to reach the protest sites? Certainly not the students.

"My fear is that innocent students will end up in jail while the real criminal elements walk free."

In Kolkata, lawyers Raja Sengupta and Syed Nafirul Islam, who have represented detained protesters pro bono, said the legal fight is far from over.

"Oppression of protesters by governments is not new," Sengupta told DW. "Our responsibility is to defend people's democratic rights. The students were protesting for a genuine cause, and they deserve legal protection."

P S Sanjeev, Kerala state secretary of the Students' Federation of India, said uncertainty remains.

"We are still trying to establish exactly which police cases have been withdrawn," Sanjeev told DW. "There is very little clarity, and many families remain anxious."

Student protesters still under pressure

Student protesters say that police action has changed rather than disappeared. Instead of large-scale arrests during demonstrations, they describe police visits to homes, questioning based on photographs and CCTV footage, continuing investigations and monitoring of social media activity.

A senior Delhi Police official rejected allegations of intimidation, saying officers were only following up on registered cases and investigating alleged offences using CCTV footage, photographs and other digital evidence.

"No one is being targeted for peaceful protest. Action is being taken strictly in accordance with the law against those suspected of criminal acts," the official told DW on condition of anonymity.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) did not respond to DW's requests for comment.

Among those who have approached the courts is Mohammad Junaid Malik, a law student who ran protest-relateda free community kitchen for protesters at Delhi's Jantar Mantar for 35 days. He has petitioned the Supreme Court, alleging illegal detention, interrogation and harassment of his family after the protests ended.

In Uttar Pradesh state, a young protester told DW anonymously that he was detained after police identified him from a photograph taken during a solidarity demonstration. Police deny any illegal detention and say individuals were questioned before being released.

In Bihar, student organizations say several protesters, including minors, were detained before the state began withdrawing protest-related cases. Police have since begun releasing detainees and removing photographs circulated to identify alleged participants in violence.

"It was an anxious wait for parents" outside the jail, Patna-based student activist Soma Roy told DW. "Many families were not even told where their children had been lodged."

Student leaders say such incidents have left many protesters uncertain whether the assurances announced by governments are being implemented on the ground.

Several Instagram users said posts and videos relating to the July demonstrations have disappeared, while CJP leaders allege police are identifying protesters through photographs, social media posts and facial recognition technology.

They argue the aim is not simply to investigate alleged offenses but to discourage future mobilization.

"We know how the police operate, and it is up to its old tricks. It is sheer bullying," Naveen Kumar, an engineering student from Delhi, told DW.

Students say police seek to prevent future protests

The result, student groups say, is a climate of fear that lingers. Particularly in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, several protesters have said they remain under watch even after the demonstrations ended. Students argue the aim is not simply to investigate alleged offenses but to discourage future mobilization.

Neha Bora, president of the All-India Students' Association (AISA), said the movement is concerned by the government's emphasis on alleged criminal records.

"That was never part of the assurances given to us," Bora, who was on a 23-day-long hunger fast, told DW.

"The police have spoken of around 2,800 protesters with criminal cases. To us, that looks like an attempt to justify the crackdown and discredit the movement," Bora said.

Bora also alleges that Muslim and Dalit students have been disproportionately targeted in some states.

"The aim is to create fear and break the unity that defined the protests," she said. "But students continue to stand together and demand the release of everyone detained."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: FIFA plans: Infantino under pressure as senior advisor quits
entries.summary: After regional football federations condemned FIFA plans for private investment, Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, tendered his resignation.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

After regional football federations condemned FIFA plans for private investment, Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, tendered his resignation.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino was under increasing pressure on Friday as global opposition grew to his controversial private investment plans and one of his senior advisors resigned in protest.

The football world was rocked earlier this week when it was reported that FIFA, the sport's global governing body, was planning to sell a stake in a new commercial subsidiary to private equity investors close to US President Donald Trump, prompting widespread outrage.

European football's governing body, UEFA, quickly condemned the plans with its 55 member associations voting unanimously to boycott future FIFA competitions — including the next men's World Cup in 2030 but potentially starting with the under-20 Women's World Cup on September 5 — were the plans to be implemented.

The Europeans soon received backing from CONCACAF, the regional body representing 41 North American and Caribbean football federations, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) with its 47 members, technically robbing Infantino of majority support among FIFA's 211 member associations (MAs).

FIFA advisor Cordeiro steps down

On Friday, the pressure on FIFA grew even more when Carlos Cordeiro, former head of the United States Soccer Federation (USSF) and more recently a senior advisor to both Infantino and President Trump during this year's men's World Cup, resigned in protest at the plans, which he described as a "bad deal for football."

In statement, Cordeiro, 69-year-old former partner at Goldman Sachs, questioned why FIFA needed to seek private equity investment at all given its unprecedented World Cup profits, and criticized a lack of transparancy, oversight and due process surrounding the plans.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources," he said. "The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt. The FIFA president himself has highlighted the $15 billion in revenue generated [during FIFA's last four-year World Cup cycle] between 2022 and 2026.

"If member associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources. Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification."

FIFA: 'Nobody is selling football'

Despite the opposition voiced by UEFA, CONCACAF, AFC and individual national associations including the German Football Federation (DFB), FIFA had earlier doubled down on its plans to establish "FIFA Forward Enterprise" (FFE).

The subsidiary, valued by FIFA at around $20 billion (€17.5 billion), would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts for its competitions, including the World Cup, but would sell a non-controling minority stake worth $4.2 billion to private equity investors.

The proposed investor consortium is expected to be led by "Thrive Eternal," a fund run by "Thrive Capital," in turn founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US ​President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

"Nobody is selling football. ‌This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA said in statement earlier on Friday, slamming "incorrect media reports" without issuing clarification and what precisely was wrongly reported, and insisting that it would proceed with its "consultation process" — with member associations obliged to make a decision by September 19.

"FIFA [member associations are] now being asked to believe that outside investors are needed to unlock greater value. I do not accept that proposition," said Cordeiro.

"Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions: Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?"

UEFA lead FIFA criticism, threaten World Cup boycott

European football's governing body UEFA, which has been at loggerheads with FIFA and Infantino for years and criticized the global body throughout the recent World Cup over expensive ticket prices and the Folarin Balogun red card affair, had come out publicly in opposition to the plan within an hour of it first being reported by the Financial Times and Times on Tuesday.

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," UEFA said in a statement after a unanimous vote by its 55 member associations at a hastily convened emergency meeting on Thursday.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product ... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale," the statement added.

Meanwhile, political criticism came from new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a keen football supporter and one of the first European leaders to criticize the FIFA plans earlier in the week,

"My view is strengthening [that] this was an outrageous suggestion," said Burnham on Friday. "The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA general secretary [Infantino] is the wrong man to lead the organization."

CONCACAF and AFC join opposition

Shortly after, North America's soccer body CONCACAF also unanimously rejected the FIFA plan, though it stopped short of threatening a boycott by its 41 members.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) also issued a scathing letter to its 47 member associations and warned the FIFA proposal would never succeed without the support of all six regional blocs.

"While the immediate debate centres on FFE, the AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal. Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed," read an AFC statement.

"This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined. Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA's governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies."

African body CAF said it would convene an executive committee meeting next week to look into the proposal, saying in a statement:

"CAF is committed to continue consulting and working together with its Member Associations, FIFA, other Football Confederations and stakeholders in support of increasing financial and other resources for the development and growth of football in Africa and worldwide," it said.

South America's CONMEBOL has yet to comment, but its president, Alejandro Dominguez, recently spoke out in favor of a further expansion of the men's World Cup to 64 teams in 2030 — which would effectively result in all but one South American nations qualifying automatically.

Amid the outrage over the investment plans, the Press Association reported on Friday that FIFA was indeed pursuing precisely such an expansion, with a decision expected by August 14.

Germany: What has the DFB said?

Germany's mass-circulation Bild paper reported that key UEFA officials including German Football Federation (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf had already discussed the FIFA plans via a video call on Wednesday.

"We must not lose the fans' support, but we are well on the way to squandering that," Neuendorf told public broadcaster ZDF, adding:

"I consider this to be extremely problematic and unacceptable. If UEFA rejects this request [for approval of the plan], then it is dead, because I believe that you won't be able to find any investor who would be willing to go ahead with this project if UEFA is out."

It's not the first time that the DFB has crossed swords with FIFA. At the Qatar World Cup in 2022, Germany's men's team covered their mouths before a game in protest at not being allowed to wear a "One Love" rainbow armband to support LGBT+ rights.

German football also has recent experience of similar private equity investment proposals. 

In 2024, the Bundesliga was forced to abandon plans to sell a share of its TV rights to foreign investors due to fan protests that included tennis balls and remote control cars with smoke bombs being thrown onto pitch during matches.

Such actions are commonplace in German football, where the so-called 50+1 ownership model bars single investors owning a majority stake in a club and ensures fans retain more power than elsewhere in the world.

Read more on Germany's response to the FIFA plans here.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Ceuta: Spain scrambles after thousands breach exclave border
entries.summary: Spanish police and troops are trying to shore up Ceuta's border to Morocco after Thursday's mass breach. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is also inbound, as Spain's neighbors implement temporary border checks. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published July 31, 2026last updated July 31, 2026

Spanish police and troops are trying to shore up Ceuta's border to Morocco after Thursday's mass breach. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is also inbound, as Spain's neighbors implement temporary border checks. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Ceuta says it cannot cope after estimated 60,000 people entered the city
  • Spain's Pedro Sanchez visits Ceuta, blames the influx on people smugglers manipulating a recent Supreme Court ruling
  • Spain's military sends personnel to assist Guardia Civil border police
  • France and Italy say they will temporarily tighten border controls at their frontiers to Spain
  • Germany's Merz calls on Morocco to take back the irregular migrants'without delay'

Follow this blog for continuing coverage and updates on the developing situation in Ceuta, Spain's North African territory.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section What, and where, is Ceuta?

What, and where, is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish exclave on North Africa's coast, bordering Morocco, not that far east of Tangiers.

It's roughly 17 kilometers (or 11 miles) away from Cadiz and the Spanish mainland, across the Strait of Gibraltar.

The city of roughly 85,000 people has a similar size and status as Melilla, further east along the coast. As well as the local autonomous administration, one lawmaker represents the territory in Spain's national parliament.

Ceuta is part of the territory of the European Union, although it's only possible to reach the Spanish mainland via ferry, with ID or passport checks nominally required in order to board.

When Spain recognized the independence of Spanish Morocco in 1956, Ceuta and other so-called "strongholds of sovereignty" (plazas de soberania) remained under Spanish control. Morocco disputed this.

Skip next section EU's von der Leyen: 'Dangerous crossings must stop immediately'

EU's von der Leyen: 'Dangerous crossings must stop immediately'

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Friday called the images coming from Ceuta unacceptable.

"We cannot allow anyone to come to our Union without abiding by our rules," she wrote online. "Dangerous crossings must stop immediately. Smuggling networks must be dismantled. And returns must be swift, as our rules allow."

Von der Leyen said she'd asked two relevant European Commissioners to provide support.

Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner was already working closely with Spain and was "ready to travel to critical points," she said.

She added that Commissioner for the Mediterranean and Demography, Dubravka Suica was "in contact with her Moroccan counterpart."

Von der Leyen said she was "confident that our close partnership with Morocco will help deliver concrete results."

Skip next section Merz calls protection of EU's external border 'decisive for the fight against illegal migration'

Merz calls protection of EU's external border 'decisive for the fight against illegal migration'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters in Berlin on Friday that Spain "wants to and must get the situation in Ceuta back under control as quickly as possible." 

He said that "the protection of the EU's external borders is decisive for the fight against illegal migration."

Merz welcomed Spain's intention to ensure the return of the new arrivals across the border to Morocco.

"We expect Morocco to take back the illegal migrants without delay," he said.

Although the exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are legally part of the Schengen Zone ← in that spending time there typically counts towards things like visa requirements — travel to mainland Spain is only possible via ferry. This means ID or passport checks are at least theoretically required in order to access the rest of the open-border Schengen Zone.

Skip next section Spain's PM Sanchez blames traffickers for spreading false rumors and triggering influx

Spain's PM Sanchez blames traffickers for spreading false rumors and triggering influx

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez described the mass crossings into Ceuta as a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity" in comments to reporters in the exclave on Friday.

Sanchez attributed the sudden increase in people seeking to swim around the border to a rumor being spread by human traffickers, deliberately misinterpreting a recent Supreme Court ruling.

A Spanish Supreme Court ruled earlier in July that immediate returns of migrants crossing the border illegally did not apply to those arriving by sea. However, the case pertained to people crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Meditereannean Sea, not people swimming around the land border to Ceuta or Melilla to enter Spain "by sea."

"What has emerged from our talks with Moroccan authorities is that trafficking mafias took a self-serving interpretation of a Supreme Court ruling," Sanchez said.

Those rumors "spread like wildfire in recent hours," he added, following the much slower start to the process earlier in the week.

Skip next section Ceuta government head estimates that 60,000 people have entered

Ceuta government head estimates that 60,000 people have entered

The head of the regional government in the autonomous city, Juan Jesus Vivas, has told reporters that crowds equivalent to well over half of Ceuta's population have entered the city.

"Estimates indicated that around 60,000 people have entered our city as a result of this event," he said. "This figure shows that it is impossible to absorb such pressure. It is absolutely impossible."

Vivas had on Thursday called on Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to declare a national emergency and to deploy military troops to assist with securing the border, issuing this appeal at roughly the same time as much larger crowds started to circumvent the border checks.

Skip next section RECAP — Tens of thousands breach border after days of people swimming into territory

RECAP — Tens of thousands breach border after days of people swimming into territory

You can catch up on our prior reporting on the issue this week here.

Authorities in Ceuta first started to note an increased number of people trying to swim around the border controls and into the territory earlier this week. But at first people were only coming in comparatively small numbers, reaching an estimated total of 1,500 to 2,000 by Thursday morning. 

On Thursday, Ceuta issued a public appeal for help from Spain.

At around the same time, much larger crowds, now estimated to number in the tens of thousands, breached the border and overwhelmed border police. 

By Friday morning, Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was en route to the exclave of around 85,000 people. Security services estimated that almost 50,000 had gained entry to Ceuta in recent days. 

Skip next section Welcome to our updates

Welcome to our updates

Hi, thanks for joining us as we continue to cover the developments in Spain's exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco on the North African coast.

entries.title: German court rules that AI music firm Suno violated copyrights
entries.summary: Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.
entries.content:
Germany

German court rules that AI music firm violated copyrights

July 31, 2026

Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.

The Munich Regional Court ruled on Friday that Suno AI, a US-based company, which generates songs from text prompts. has violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues.

The lawsuit initiated in January 2025 by GEMA, Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, argued that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.

According to the ‌verdict, Suno will have to pay damages that have yet to be quantified. Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.

"This is a verdict of global significance," Gema CEO Tobias Holzmueller told Reuters.

A closely watched case

The lawsuit has been closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs. Among Suno's arguments was the fact that the German court does not have proper jurisdiction to rule on AI model training activities that occurred exclusively inside the United States.

The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

"Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller, who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models." He believes Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

The outcome of this case is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?

At the forefront of the battle to protect artists' rights

Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court. It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization. 

OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages. But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW. "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer. And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."

GEMA represents more than 95,000 composers, songwriters and music publishers in Germany, along with over 2 million rights holders worldwide.

How did GEMA present its case?

GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society. GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

Suno's music creation platform generates songs through simple text prompts. Users can describe the mood, style or genre they desire and the system synthesizes a structured track — complete with lyrics, vocals and instrumentation — in under a minute.

The songs that are produced by the AI system can be very similar to copyrighted songs.

During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.

Along with the lyrics, the plaintiffs prompted the desired musical style and the title of the work, without specifying any melody, rhythm, harmony or arrangement.

Yet the resulting AI songs are very similar to the original works.

Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally. In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

"The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben. By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.

Why AI shouldn't be compared to human brains

Anyone who wants to become a good musician needs to listen to and learn from existing music.

Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.

But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller. "These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds. I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.

"To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day. Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller. "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

"If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA. "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

For example, music in movie scores or social media has until recently allowed various songwriters to make a living. For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field. "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."

This article was originally published on July 30, 2026 and was updated on July 31, 2026 to reflect the court's ruling.

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Military flare-up between Houthis and Saudi Arabia challenges relative calm in Yemen
entries.summary: Riyadh and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are on the brink of renewed conflict. Could war-ravaged Yemen be drawn into a wider Middle East war?
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Tensions rise between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia

July 31, 2026

Riyadh and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are on the brink of renewed conflict. Could war-ravaged Yemen be drawn into a wider Middle East war?

Military strikes between Yemen's ruling Houthi militia and Saudi Arabia have flared for the first time since the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Houthis agreed to a truce in 2022.

Tensions rose earlier in July when the Iran-backed Houthi group claimed that Saudi Arabia had struck the airport in Sanaa to prevent Houthi leaders from returning after the funeral of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. Saudi Arabia, for its part, has denied the attack and claimed that the Houthis were spreading false claims.

Since then, the Houthis have struck facilities owned by Saudi Arabia's national oil company, Aramco, forcing the Jazan production site to shut down. The blow hit Saudi Arabia particularly hard as Jazan has been serving as an export hub to circumvent Iran's ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis also announced that they would block Saudi-linked commercial vessels from passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden — prompting several ships to turn back this week. The narrow strait has become more significant for Saudi oil exports due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis said they fired missiles at the oil tanker NCC Ghazal.

Riyadh, meanwhile, confirmed it had struck Houthi targets in response to the threats to Red Sea shipping. On Thursday, Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry announced that it was establishing a multinational defense maritime coalition to protect key shipping routes. According to the statement on X, 14 countries had already confirmed participation.

Will Yemen be dragged into the wider US-Israel war in Iran?

"The current escalation appears to be driven primarily by the Houthis," Elham Manea, a political scientist and adjunct professor at the University of Zurich specializing in Middle East and Gulf studies, told DW.

For her, it is increasingly obvious that the Houthis, who are part of Tehran's "Axis of Resistance" — Iran's paramilitary proxy groups including Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and Shiite militias in Iraq who all call for the elimination of the United States and Israel —  have  abandoned their strategy to refrain from joining the wider US-Iran war.

The conflict, which began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, has since engulfed much of the Middle East. This week, Saudi Arabia also joined US forces in striking infrastructure used by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

"The Houthis are now using the wider US–Iran confrontation to revive unresolved issues with Saudi Arabia," Manea said, noting that "the Houthi strategy is to raise costs for Riyadh and strengthen their own bargaining position."

She added that Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi's recent speeches are quite revealing in this respect. "While they express solidarity with Iran, they increasingly justify escalation through specifically Yemeni demands directed at Riyadh."

Above all, the Houthis want Saudi Arabia to end its air and sea blockades on Houthi-held territory which have not been fully lifted despite the truce in 2022.

Some hesitation to return to a full-scale war

Despite the current escalation, it is still too early to conclude that Saudi Arabia has abandoned its policy of restraint in Yemen, Manea cautioned. "Since the 2022 truce, Riyadh's priority has been to extricate itself from the Yemen war and create the regional stability needed for its broader economic transformation 'Vision 2030'," Manea said.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict monitoring watchdog ACLED, also still sees some leverage before a return to a full-scale war. "The Houthis have left some room for de-escalation," he noted in a recent analysis. Two ships bound for China carrying Saudi crude passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait without incident on 23 July, suggesting that at least some ships are exempt from the Houthi blockade, he wrote.

Michael Stephens, senior Middle East security advisor at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, points to previous experiences between the factions. "If Saudi Arabia and the Houthis go back to war in Yemen, I suspect the ending will be the same: A lot of money spent, many lives lost, and eventually the realization that both sides will have to talk," he told DW. In his view, the Houthis are unlikely to be defeated without a costly invasion.

The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and Saudi Arabia escalated in 2015 when Saudi Arabia joined the war in Yemen in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Since the truce in 2022, the Houthis have largely consolidated their position as the de facto rulers of Yemen. However, the country remains divided: The Houthis control the capital Sanaa, most of northern Yemen and parts of the center. The UN-recognized government, now based primarily in Aden and exiled in Saudi Arabia, controls parts of the south and east, while the separatist Southern Transitional Council dominates much of the south. Tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

Fighting exacerbates Yemen's dire humanitarian situation

Human rights organizations point out that the population is yet to recover from those years of devastating war. According to the United Nations, Yemen is still suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

"Since 2014, the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis have destroyed food and water infrastructure across Yemen and they have also blocked food, fuel, and humanitarian aid from reaching segments of the population," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "The impact on the population has been clear," she said.

The conflict has left more than half of the population without adequate access to basic food needs and many people are already on the brink of starvation, Jafarnia told DW. Her worry is that "as warring parties escalate the conflict again, there is a real risk that they will also again weaponize civilians' basic needs."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer
